case_study_insert.main_stem: Gingerfield Craft Beverages (GCB) is a partnership in the craft soft-drinks sector, based near the Great Lakes and employing a workforce of 45. Founded in 2013 by brothers Daniel and Samuel Okafor, it supplies ginger beer to independent retailers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. GCB plans to invest $540,000 in a new bottling and canning line, financed by a $340,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.90 a unit and a selling price of $8.40, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. GCB faces rising waste: 2.8% of cans fail the fill-level check and labour turnover is increasing.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The canning line filled 23,400 units last quarter with a waste rate of 2.8%, down from 4.3% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 30 to 18 per month. Average delivery lead time is 2.9 days. A survey of 640 shoppers found that 74% would pay up to $0.35 more for naturally sweetened ginger beer, and 62% check ingredient labels. Records show 15 of 45 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new filler; off-the-job training courses at the community college cost $820 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Gingerfield Craft Beverages as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.5% to 4.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $11.50 to $12.29 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale ginger, sugar and aluminium can input costs have risen 11.5% year-on-year, food inflation is 5.7%, and consumer spending on craft soft drinks grew 4.4%.

questions.question_text: GCB plans to fund part of its canning-line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for GCB of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest or capital repayments, protecting the cash flow of a partnership with fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a variable cost of $3.90 a unit. The $200,000 of retained profit is already in the business, so cash that would have gone to the $340,000 bank loan can be spent on reducing the 2.8% waste rate at the filler or on absorbing the 11.5% rise in ginger, sugar and aluminium can costs without raising the $8.40 selling price.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps decision-making with Daniel and Samuel Okafor, with no lender covenants restricting how the $540,000 bottling and canning line is run — important for a flat structure with democratic leadership. It also avoids the collateral and default risk of the bank loan: if independent retailers cut orders, the equipment cannot be repossessed, and the project can begin immediately without the delay of loan approval while the 23,400-unit quarterly run rate is maintained.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to GCB and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: GCB is launching a new naturally sweetened ginger beer. Consider local food festivals, regional radio advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should GCB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local food festivals: Festivals let GCB pour samples for shoppers near the Great Lakes, get immediate feedback and build local loyalty, which suits a partnership selling to independent retailers. The drawback is cost in staff time and travel for a 45-person firm funding a $540,000 line, and each event reaches only a small local crowd, so it cannot support the 90,000-unit output target.

Regional radio advertising: Radio is relatively inexpensive and can repeat the naturally sweetened message across the region, supporting independent retailers near the Great Lakes. Its limits are reach and proof: audio cannot show ingredient labels that 62% of 640 surveyed shoppers check, and most potential buyers of craft soft drinks are beyond any single regional station.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and drink influencers can show the product and explain natural sweetening visually to a targeted national audience, with measurable engagement and low cost per impression. Credibility must be managed and results build over time, but the 74% of shoppers who would pay $0.35 more can be addressed directly and repeatedly.

Recommendation: GCB should choose social media influencer marketing, with a few local festivals to keep retailer relationships warm. It reaches the researched 74% premium segment nationally and shows the labels that radio cannot. Radio is rejected as narrow and unable to prove the ingredient story; festivals alone are rejected as too small-scale for 90,000 units and a $340,000 loan commitment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GCB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GCB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and festivals are rejected.

questions.question_text: GCB's waste rate is 2.8% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for GCB of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its production staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 45 employees a say in how the new bottling and canning line is organised, which suits a flat structure and raises job satisfaction. Operators who help set fill-level routines can suggest practical fixes that build on the fall in waste from 4.3% to 2.8%, protecting the $8.40 selling price and the relationship with independent retailers.

Point 2: Consulting the team also helps tackle rising labour turnover by letting staff influence shift patterns and training, reducing the disruption that absence causes on a 90,000-unit line with fixed costs of $180,000 a year. With 15 of 45 staff still untrained on the filler, listening to operators helps target on-the-job training properly while the $540,000 line beds in and the $340,000 loan is serviced.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GCB's waste, staffing and output.

questions.question_text: GCB must upskill 15 staff to operate the new filler. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the community college. Which should GCB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching the 15 untrained staff beside the filler is directly relevant to GCB's own fill-level standards and costs no course fees, unlike the $820 per employee charged by the community college. It keeps all 15 workers productive while they learn, protecting the 23,400 units filled last quarter and the improvement in waste from 4.3% to 2.8%. The drawbacks are that trainers have their own work to do and bad habits can spread without formal assessment.

Off-the-job training: The $820 per employee college course gives structured teaching and a recognised certificate for all 15 staff, costing $12,300 in total — small against the $540,000 investment. It removes 15 of 45 workers from the line, cutting short-term capacity and risking the 2.8% waste target, and generic content may not match GCB's filler settings without follow-up coaching.

Decision: GCB should choose on-the-job training first, adding short college modules for senior operators later. It is cheapest, machine-specific and protects output while waste is only just improving; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing $12,300 and 15 of 45 staff would disrupt supply to independent retailers when the $340,000 loan must be serviced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to GCB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of GCB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of GCB with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GCB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($8.40 − $3.90) = $180,000 ÷ $4.50 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $8.40 − $3.90 = $4.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GCB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 40,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 90,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 50,000 units, to judge whether the $540,000 canning line is justified.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.50 lets GCB model the $0.35 naturally sweetened premium: if 74% of surveyed shoppers accept it, managers can weigh the extra contribution against the 11.5% input-cost rise.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $180,000 and contribution helps set the volume needed to service interest on the $340,000 bank loan before the partnership borrows more.
4. Unit cost can be checked as $180,000 ÷ 90,000 + $3.90 = $5.90, and labour productivity as 90,000 units ÷ 45 staff = 2,000 units per worker, giving benchmarks to track the 2.8% waste rate and rising labour turnover.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 50,000 units vs 90,000 output; the $0.35 premium against $180,000 fixed costs; loan servicing on the $340,000 bank loan; and unit cost of $5.90 with labour productivity of 2,000 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GCB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GCB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.84 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.13 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $62,000 inventories + $98,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $190,000; 2025 current assets = $50,000 + $110,000 + $45,000 = $205,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $190,000 ÷ $152,000 = 1.25 and 2025 = $205,000 ÷ $137,000 = 1.50. Excluding inventories gives 2024 = ($190,000 − $62,000) ÷ $152,000 = $128,000 ÷ $152,000 = 0.84 and 2025 = ($205,000 − $50,000) ÷ $137,000 = $155,000 ÷ $137,000 = 1.13.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The 2024 figure of 1.25 rose to 1.50 because current assets rose from $190,000 to $205,000 while current liabilities fell from $152,000 to $137,000, helped by cash rising from $30,000 to $45,000. The inventory-excluding measure improved from 0.84 to 1.13, so GCB can meet short-term debts without relying on selling canned stock while it services a $340,000 loan and funds a $540,000 line. There is a caveat: receivables rose from $98,000 to $110,000, so cash may be tied up if independent retailers pay late, and inventories fell to $50,000, which supports the 23,400-unit quarterly run rate but leaves a thin buffer if the 2.8% waste rate worsens.

Conclusion: GCB's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the gain does not depend on inventory. The residual risk is slower-paying retailers, so the partners should tighten credit control while the new canning line operates.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether GCB's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GCB of introducing naturally sweetened ingredients in its ginger beer.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Natural sweetening matches the 74% of 640 surveyed shoppers who would pay up to $0.35 more, protecting the $4.50 contribution per unit while ginger, sugar and aluminium can costs rise 11.5%. It also appeals to the 62% who check ingredient labels, strengthening the brand with independent retailers and supporting the $540,000 canning investment.

Disadvantage: Natural sweeteners often cost more than standard sugar, which could push up the $3.90 variable cost per unit unless the $0.35 premium is accepted across the whole range. A supply problem with natural ingredients could also cut the 23,400 units filled each quarter and push waste above 2.8%, while fixed costs of $180,000 continue regardless of output.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GCB's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.25%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 11.5% rise in ginger, sugar and can input costs will affect GCB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.5% to 4.25%): The base rate rises by 0.75 percentage points. If the $340,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.0075 × $340,000 = $2,550 a year, which is modest beside fixed costs of $180,000 a year, and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates could make consumers more cautious about craft soft drinks, but GCB can largely remove the direct effect by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, from $11.50 to $12.29 per hour): This raises the wage bill for a 45-person workforce and cannot be avoided. The insert provides no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so an annual wage total would be an invention. The comparison that can be derived is productivity: 90,000 units ÷ 45 staff = 2,000 units per worker. If that is maintained the rise is absorbable; if labour turnover cuts output, unit labour cost rises and the $4.50 contribution per unit narrows.

Input cost inflation (11.5% on ginger, sugar and aluminium cans): The insert does not decompose the $3.90 variable cost, so only a labelled bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 11.5%, that adds 0.115 × $3.90 = $0.45 per unit, and at 90,000 units a year that is about $40,365. This is an upper bound, not a prediction; the true figure depends on the ingredient share of variable cost, which is not stated. GCB can recover part through the $0.35 premium accepted by 74% of surveyed shoppers.

Conclusion: The 11.5% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it applies to every can and attacks the $4.50 contribution that supports the $540,000 line, whereas the interest effect of $2,550 is small and fixable and the wage effect can be offset if 2,000-units-per-worker productivity holds. Input-cost inflation therefore requires the strongest management response.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GCB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GCB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GCB with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
